query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the multi‐phase eutectic HEA, mechanical wear at elevated temperature disrupts the evolving passive film at multiphase boundaries, exposing chemically active fresh surfaces that are more susceptible to corrosion. This localized film removal initiates a feedback loop where corrosion accelerates after exposing vulnerable interfaces, and the resulting structural degradation further promotes wear, thereby synergistically accelerating the overall degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with an engineered microstructure that, under non-wear conditions, develops an in situ protective passive film at phase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Conduct a controlled variable experiment where one set of samples is subjected to sliding wear (via varying applied load/speed) in a corrosive, elevated-temperature environment, while a matched control set experiences only the corrosive environment without mechanical wear.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature in a chloride-containing corrosive environment, with wear imposed through controlled sliding conditions to selectively disrupt surface films at multiphase boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity of the passive protection film at the multiphase boundaries
generation.mechanism: Wear disrupts the passive film, exposing clean, chemically active surfaces at the interfaces of different phases. These areas, having high interfacial potential differences, undergo accelerated localized galvanic corrosion. As corrosion further degrades the surface, the weakened areas are more prone to mechanical removal, reinforcing the cycle of degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the non-wear baseline, samples under simultaneous wear and corrosion will show a significantly higher total degradation, characterized by an increased corrosion rate (due to localized film breakdown) and augmented wear rates (from compromised surface integrity).
generation.baseline: The same HEA alloy exposed to the corrosion environment at elevated temperature without the application of mechanical wear, maintaining an intact passive film.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to dominate under conditions where the temperature enables both robust film formation and rapid film breakdown, the mechanical load is sufficient to induce wear at the film interfaces, and the environment provides aggressive ionic species (e.g., Cl−) that drive localized corrosion.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative rates of acceleration in corrosion and wear remain uncertain. Variations in alloy composition or slight differences in microstructural features could modify the resilience of the passive film and hence the synergistic effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical multi‐phase eutectic HEA samples. Expose one set to a controlled sliding wear regime while both sets are immersed in a chloride-containing electrolyte at elevated temperature. Use in situ surface characterization methods (such as electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy) to monitor the integrity of the passive film, and measure corrosion currents and wear volumes for both sets.
measurements: Passive film continuity and composition (via XPS/EIS)
Wear track morphology and volume loss
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples experiencing mechanical wear do not show a statistically significant decrease in passive film integrity, no marked increase in localized corrosion current relative to the no-wear control, and if the overall degradation rate is not synergistically higher (i.e., exceeds the additive effects of separate wear and corrosion), then the hypothesis that wear-induced film disruption accelerates coupled degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

frame.system: A multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with an engineered multiphase microstructure as its initial state, designed for robust performance but now challenged by simultaneous wear and corrosion at high temperature.
frame.goal: To identify a single mechanistic hypothesis that explains the accelerated, coupled degradation (i.e. synergistic wear–corrosion) under elevated temperature conditions and to predict how the overall degradation and its individual wear and corrosion components differ from a matched baseline.
frame.limitation: The current lack of an integrated mechanism that accounts for the interaction between wear and corrosion at high temperature in multiphase, eutectic high‐entropy alloys, leading to unpredictable accelerated degradation.
constraints: Must be a single mechanistic explanation
Requires a controlled comparison to distinguish the hypothesis from baseline effects
The hypothesis should define clear boundary conditions
Must include a falsification criterion and supporting evidence
frame.regime: Operating under conditions of high temperature in an environment where mechanical wear (tribological stress) and electrochemical corrosion occur concurrently.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have separately examined wear and corrosion mechanisms in these materials, which failed to capture the synergistic effects under simultaneous exposure.
Standard baseline comparisons without accounting for interactive degradation mechanisms could not predict the accelerated overall degradation.
frame.understanding: The hypothesis should articulate how interactions between wear-induced surface damage and the formation/disruption of corrosion protective films accelerate degradation. For example, it might propose that wear removes the evolving passive film at the multiphase boundaries, exposing fresh material that corrodes more rapidly. This exposes harder phases to preferential mechanical removal and corrosion, leading to a feedback loop that accelerates the overall material loss.

decision.trend: Initial investigations into high-entropy alloys focused on their phase-engineered microstructures and high-temperature mechanical properties. Early work predominantly treated wear and corrosion as separate degradation modes, with studies examining how microstructural design (eutectic architectures, nanohierarchical structures) could individually optimize wear resistance or corrosion performance. In later studies, researchers began to note that in dynamic environments, the formation and rupture of surface oxide films—particularly at the multiphase boundaries—could couple mechanical wear with enhanced corrosion, as the removal of a protective film exposed fresh, chemically active interfaces. However, these studies did not culminate in a single, unified mechanistic hypothesis that captures the synergistic interaction between wear-induced film breakdown and accelerated corrosion under high-temperature conditions.
decision.unsolved: A unified explanation that directly links the wear-induced removal of evolving passive or protective films (particularly at multiphase interfaces) to a localized enhancement of corrosion in eutectic high-entropy alloys at elevated temperatures remains unaddressed. The challenge is to correlate mechanical film disruption with the subsequent exposure of chemically vulnerable surfaces that accelerate degradation, under clearly defined controlled conditions.
decision.lever: Implement a systematic experimental design that independently controls sliding wear rates (e.g., by varying load and speed) and electrochemical conditions (e.g., maintaining fixed potential or modulated polarization) while monitoring in situ the integrity of the passive film via advanced surface characterization. Key parameters include the rate of film removal, the reformation kinetics of the passive film at multiphase boundaries, and the resulting localized corrosion currents under elevated temperatures.
decision.why: This controlled comparison directly isolates the effect of wear-induced passive film disruption from other baseline degradation processes. By comparing samples with intentionally varied wear conditions against matched non-wear controls, the experiment can verify whether accelerated corrosion is indeed a consequence of mechanical removal of protective films—a hypothesis that aligns precisely with the observed coupled degradation trends and the theoretical gap in current understanding.
